Agree a two-minute review with two questions only: what actually happened, and what would a kind observer say. Then a physical switch. Practice on the last event the client replayed.

fields.label: The event I keep replaying
What I replay most (a sentence, a look, a pause)
My two-minute review: what actually happened
What a kind observer would say
My switch when the two minutes are up
How long the replay used to last, and how long it lasted this time

title: Social Prediction Log
summary: Records the client's forecast before a social situation and the outcome after, to compare over weeks.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that their predictions run far worse than events.
body_md: The forecast must be specific and rated: they will notice me blushing and think less of me, seventy percent. Afterward the client records what observably happened, not how it felt. Review the gap across ten entries, which is usually where belief shifts rather than in any single event.

fields.label: The upcoming situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
What observably happened
How I know (what people said or did)
How the prediction compared
What I predict next time, adjusted

title: Conversation Toolkit Card
summary: A pocket card of openers, follow-up questions and graceful exits for social situations.
goal: Reduce the load of inventing conversation so the client can practice being in it.
body_md: Build it with the client's own words, not scripts from a book, and include exits, since knowing they can leave makes staying easier. Warn against using it as a safety behavior: the card is for learning, and the goal is to need it less. Rehearse a full opener-question-exit in session.

fields.label: Three openers I could actually say
Three follow-up questions that work in most conversations
Two ways to leave a conversation gracefully
What I will do with my hands
The one I will try first this week
How it went, and whether I needed the card

title: Social Brave Steps for Teens
summary: A teen's own ladder of social situations from easy to hard, with a brave step per week.
goal: Give a teenager a graded, self-chosen path back into the social situations they have been dodging.
body_md: Let the teen build and order the steps; a ladder chosen by an adult will not be climbed. Keep parents to a support role agreed on the sheet. Steps should be specific: ask one question in class, not participate more. Celebrate attempts, not outcomes, and expect a step to be repeated before moving up.

fields.label: Situations I have been avoiding
My ladder, easiest at the bottom
This week's step
What I am afraid will happen
What actually happened
What my parent will do (and not do) to help
The step for next week

title: Continuing Bonds Letter
summary: A letter to the person who died, about what has happened since and what the client still carries of them.
goal: Support an ongoing connection with the person rather than a closing of the door.
body_md: Offer it as one option among several, since some clients find writing to the dead unbearable and others find it the only thing that helps. Frame the bond as something that changes rather than ends. The client decides whether to read it aloud, keep it, or take it somewhere. Include 988 among the prompts for the darkest hours.

fields.label: What I want to tell you about since you died
What I have kept of you (a habit, a phrase, an object, a way of seeing)
What I wish I had said
What I think you would say to me now
How I will keep you in my life going forward
If the grief ever gets dangerously dark: 988 (call or text), and who else I will reach

title: Grief Triggers Calendar
summary: A year at a glance with the dates, seasons and events likely to bring the grief up hard.
goal: Let the client see the hard days coming and plan support for them instead of being ambushed.
body_md: Include the obvious dates and the sideways ones: the first snow, the tax season the person used to handle, the song at the store. Plan for the week before an anniversary, which is often worse than the day. Decide with the client who will know about each date.

fields.label: Anniversaries and birthdays
Seasons, holidays and rituals that will be different
Sideways reminders I can predict
The next hard date, and what I will do that day
Who will know it is coming
What helped on the last hard date, and what did not

title: Dual Process Week Planner
summary: A week planned with time for facing the loss and time for the ordinary business of living, both on purpose.
goal: Normalize moving between grief and daily life instead of feeling guilty about either.
body_md: Explain that healthy grief moves between the loss and the rest of life, and that neither side is avoidance. Clients stuck on one side feel guilty when they laugh, or numb when they cannot cry; the planner gives both permission. Keep the entries small and concrete.

fields.label: Times this week I will let myself be with the loss (looking at photos, visiting, talking about them)
Times this week I will do ordinary or even pleasant things
The side I tend to get stuck on
What guilt says when I switch sides
What I will say back to it
How the week went

title: Memory Box Project
summary: A child decorates a box and fills it with objects, drawings and stories that hold the person who died.
goal: Give a grieving child a concrete, permitted place for their memories and a way to talk about them.
body_md: Let the child lead on what goes in and what stays private. Each item comes with a story the child tells if they want to; the telling is the work. Involve the surviving parent or carer where possible, and coach them to follow the child's pace rather than their own. Revisit the box on hard dates.

fields.label: What my box looks like
The first three things I put in it, and why
A story that goes with one of them
Something I want to ask about the person who died
Who I can open the box with
When I might want to open it

title: Grief Conversation Cards
summary: A deck of gentle prompts about the person who died, drawn in turn by family members or a group.
goal: Let a family or group talk about the person in a structured, low-pressure way.
body_md: Write the prompts with the group first so nothing on a card ambushes anyone, mixing light ones with heavier ones. Any card can be passed. Play in a circle with a talking object. In families, children often answer more freely than adults, which gives the adults permission.

fields.label: Prompts we put on the cards
The card I drew, and what I said
Something I learned about the person from someone else
A card I passed on
The card I would like to answer next time

title: Needs Inventory for Partners
summary: Each partner lists their needs in the relationship, ranked, and guesses their partner's list before comparing.
goal: Replace assumed needs with stated ones, and show each partner what the other has been guessing.
body_md: Have both partners complete it separately, including the guess about each other, before any discussion. The gaps between the guess and the real list are the material. Keep the tone of curiosity when a partner's need surprises the other; surprise is information, not an accusation.

fields.label: My top five needs in this relationship, ranked
How well each is being met right now (0-10)
What I think my partner's top five are
What surprised me about their real list
One need of theirs I could meet better this month
One need of mine I will ask for directly

title: Perpetual Problems Sorter
summary: Sorts a couple's recurring arguments into the solvable and the perpetual, and plans a different approach to each.
goal: Stop a couple from trying to solve what needs managing, and from managing what could be solved.
body_md: List the arguments first, then sort. Perpetual problems come from differences in personality or values and will be there in ten years; the goal is dialogue and humor about them, not a fix. Solvable problems get a concrete plan. Most couples are relieved to hear that having perpetual problems is normal.

fields.label: Arguments we have more than once a month
Which of these come from a difference in who we are
Which could actually be solved with a plan
For one solvable problem: our plan
For one perpetual problem: what we can each accept
How we will talk about the perpetual one next time it comes up

title: Trust Rebuilding Steps
summary: A shared ladder of specific, observable actions that would rebuild trust after a breach, with a timeline.
goal: Turn a vague demand to earn trust back into steps both partners can see happening.
body_md: The hurt partner names what would help; the other partner says what they can commit to. Steps must be observable, since promises to change are not. Agree how long the checking phase lasts, because trust cannot rebuild under permanent surveillance. Review progress monthly in session.

fields.label: What was broken, in one sentence each
Actions that would help me trust again (specific and visible)
Which of these I can commit to, and when
What transparency looks like for now, and for how long
What I need to hear when I have a wobble
How we will mark progress

title: Communication Pattern Replay
summary: Replays one recent exchange line by line, with each partner naming what they meant and what they heard.
goal: Show a couple the gap between what was said, what was meant and what landed.
body_md: Pick a short exchange, not the biggest fight. Write the actual lines, then have each partner add what they meant and what they heard. The gaps are usually where the fight lives. Finish by rewriting two lines each, and rehearse the rewrite in session.

fields.label: The exchange, line by line, as it happened
For my lines: what I meant
For their lines: what I heard
Where the gap between meant and heard was widest
Two lines I would rewrite
How the rewritten version sounds out loud

title: Relationship Values Compass
summary: Each partner names the kind of partner they want to be, separately from how the other is behaving.
goal: Anchor each partner to their own values so change does not wait on the other person moving first.
body_md: Works with a couple or with one partner alone. The key move is separating my values as a partner from what I get back; clients often discover they have been acting on a scoreboard. Choose one valued action for the week that does not depend on the other person's response.

fields.label: The partner I want to be, in three words
How I have actually been acting lately
What I have been waiting for my partner to do first
One valued action I will take this week regardless
What my mind says will happen if I go first
What actually happened

title: Safety and Stabilization Plan
summary: A plan for the practical and emotional safety a survivor needs in place before any deeper work.
goal: Put steady ground under the client first: who, where, what, and what to do when it gets too much.
body_md: Complete it together in session and never as homework. Cover present-day safety from the person who harmed them, the people who help, the skills that bring them back, and what to do in the worst hours. Move at the client's pace and do not ask for the details of what happened; that is not what this sheet is for. Include 988.

fields.label: Am I safe from the person now? What would make me safer
People I trust, and what each one can help with
Skills that bring me back when I am flooded
Signs that I am doing too much too fast
What I will do in the worst hour: 988 (call or text), and my other numbers
What I want my therapist to know about pace
What I am not ready to talk about yet, and that is fine

title: Consent and Boundaries Map
summary: Maps the client's yes, no and maybe across touch, closeness and conversation, in their own words.
goal: Help a survivor reclaim the right to decide, in small everyday ways, what they allow and what they do not.
body_md: Keep it to everyday boundaries at first: hugs, sitting close, questions from family, who has their number. The maybe column matters, since survivors often feel boundaries must be absolute to count. Rehearse one no in session. Nothing here asks about the abuse itself.

fields.label: Things I am a clear yes to
Things I am a clear no to
Things that are a maybe, and what would make them a yes
A boundary someone in my life keeps crossing
How I will say no to that, in my words
What I will do if they push
Someone who respects my boundaries well

title: Shame Response Sheet
summary: Catches the self-blame that follows abuse, tests it against what the client would say to another survivor, and writes the fairer version.
goal: Loosen the belief that the client caused, allowed or deserved what happened.
body_md: Do this in session, gently, and expect the double standard to be stark: the client will extend to another survivor a compassion they refuse themselves. Do not argue the client out of the belief; let the comparison do the work, and rate belief before and after. Stop if the client becomes flooded and return to grounding.

fields.label: What I tell myself about why it happened
How much I believe that (0-100%)
What I would say to a friend who told me the same story
Where the blame actually belongs
The fairer statement, in my words
How much I believe the fairer statement now (0-100%)

title: Support Disclosure Planner
summary: Plans whether, who, when and how much to tell, so a disclosure happens on the client's terms.
goal: Keep the choice of who knows, and how much, in the survivor's hands.
body_md: Not telling is a valid outcome of this sheet and should be said out loud. Work through what the client wants from telling, who is likely to respond well, and how much to say; a first sentence and an exit line are worth rehearsing. Plan for the reaction being disappointing, since it sometimes is.

fields.label: What I hope telling someone would give me
People I might tell, and how I think each would respond
The person I would tell first, if anyone
How much I want to say (a sentence is enough)
My first sentence
How I will end the conversation if I need to
What I will do for myself afterward, whatever their reaction

title: Body Safety Rules Poster
summary: A child makes a poster of body safety rules: private parts, okay and not-okay touch, secrets versus surprises, and who to tell.
goal: Teach a child the words and the permission to tell, as part of prevention work with families.
body_md: A prevention and education tool, done with a parent in the room where possible. Use correct names for body parts. Teach that surprises are fun and short and secrets about bodies are never kept. List five trusted adults. If a child discloses during this, stop the activity, stay calm, believe them, and follow your mandated reporting duties.

fields.label: Private parts have proper names, and mine are
Okay touch and not-okay touch: my examples
The difference between a surprise and a secret
My five trusted grown-ups
What I say if someone breaks a body safety rule
Where my poster will hang

title: Coping Menu by Situation
summary: A menu of the client's coping options sorted by where they are: at work, in public, at home, in bed.
goal: Match skills to settings so the right one is available where the distress actually happens.
body_md: Most clients have skills that only work at home and distress that happens elsewhere. Sort by setting and check that each setting has at least two options that are invisible to other people. Include one for the middle of the night. Keep the menu in the phone's notes.

fields.label: At work or school: two things I can do without anyone noticing
In public: two options
At home: two options
In bed at 3 a.m.: two options
The skill I reach for too often, and where it does not work
The new skill I will try this week, and where

title: Skill Practice Log
summary: A weekly log of which coping skill the client used, in what situation, and how well it worked.
goal: Turn coping from a vague resolve into a tracked practice with results.
body_md: The rating is the useful part: a skill that scores three out of ten in three different situations can be retired without guilt. Look for the mismatch between skills tried and situations faced. Praise the attempt, especially when the skill did not work, since trying is what builds the habit.

fields.label: Date and the situation
Distress before (0-10)
The skill I used
Distress after (0-10)
How well it worked (0-10) and why
A skill I could have used instead
The skill I will practice most next week

title: Coping Ladder for Kids
summary: A ladder of a child's coping moves from small feelings at the bottom to big ones at the top.
goal: Match the size of the coping move to the size of the feeling, in a picture a child can use.
body_md: Draw a ladder with three or four rungs and let the child assign feelings sizes to each. Small feelings get small moves: a breath, a drink of water. Big feelings get big moves: a break, a grown-up. Practice one move per rung in session and have the parent post the ladder at home.

fields.label: Bottom rung: a small feeling and my small move
Middle rung: a medium feeling and my medium move
Top rung: a huge feeling and my biggest move
How I know which rung I am on
Who helps me on the top rung
Where my ladder is posted

title: Coping Skills Relay
summary: Teams race to act out or demonstrate a coping skill for each situation card drawn.
goal: Rehearse coping skills under mild pressure and laughter, so they are practiced rather than just known.
body_md: Write situation cards with the group beforehand: a test tomorrow, a friend ignoring a text, a loud house. A team scores when the skill fits the situation and could actually be done there. Judge fit, not speed, and let the group argue the call; the argument is the learning.

fields.label: Situation cards we made
Skills my team demonstrated
A skill another team showed that I want to steal
A situation none of us could match well
The skill I will practice this week

title: Helpful vs Costly Coping Sort
summary: Sorts everything the client does to feel better into what helps in the long run and what costs more than it gives.
goal: Help the client judge coping by its long-term workability rather than by how fast it works.
body_md: List everything without judgment first, including the ones the client is ashamed of; those are usually the fastest-acting. Sort by long-term workability, not by how they look. Most clients find a few things belong in both columns depending on amount, which is worth writing down rather than resolving.

fields.label: Everything I do to feel better, fast or slow
Which ones help me next week too
Which ones cost more than they give
Which ones depend on how much
One costly one I will shrink, and how
One helpful one I will do more of, and when

title: Phobia Prediction Tracker
summary: Records what the client expects to happen around the feared object or situation and what actually occurs.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that the feared outcome and the felt danger diverge.
body_md: Ask for the specific feared outcome, not just fear: I will faint, the dog will bite, the plane will crash. Rate belief before and after each approach. The pattern across entries is what changes belief, so aim for at least eight entries before drawing conclusions together.

fields.label: The feared thing and the situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
Peak fear (0-10)
What actually happened
What I did during the peak
My belief in the prediction now (0-100%)

title: Approach Steps Planner
summary: Plans the next approach step toward a feared object in detail: where, how long, with whom, and what to drop.
goal: Make each approach step concrete enough to actually happen this week.
body_md: One step at a time, planned to the minute. Include what safety moves the client will drop, since carrying the escape plan into the step blunts it. Decide in advance how long to stay: long enough for the fear to fall, not just to touch and run. Debrief in session before planning the next.

fields.label: This week's step
Where and when, exactly
Who will be there, and what they will and will not do
How long I will stay (until fear drops by half)
The safety moves I will not use
What happened, and what I will do next week

title: Phobia Body Response Sheet
summary: Names what the client's body does around the feared thing, and separates the alarm from the danger.
goal: Help the client see the fear response as an alarm that can fire without a fire.
body_md: Map the response: heart, breath, muscles, stomach, the urge to run. Explain plainly that the body's alarm is doing its job and that the job is to get them out, which is why staying feels wrong. For blood or needle fears, note the faint response and plan applied tension separately.

fields.label: What my body does first around the feared thing
What it does next
The urge that comes with it
What the alarm is trying to make me do
What I know about the real danger in this situation
What I will do with the alarm next time it fires

title: Brave Practice Chart for Kids
summary: A sticker chart for a child's repeated brave practices with a feared thing, tied to a small reward.
goal: Make repetition of approach steps visible and rewarding for a child.
duration: 20 minutes to set up, then daily
body_md: Choose practices small enough to repeat daily: look at a picture of a dog, stand in the doorway with the lights off. Stickers go on for attempts, not for calm. Parents hold the chart and the reward and keep their own anxiety out of the practice. Change the practice when it stops earning fear.

fields.label: My brave practice this week
Stickers I earned
How scared I was the first time (0-10) and the last time
My reward when the chart is full
What my grown-up does during practice
Next week's brave practice

title: Fear Ladder Card Sort
summary: Situations written on cards and physically sorted into a ladder from least to most scary.
goal: Build a fear hierarchy as a hands-on sorting task rather than a form.
body_md: Write one situation per card with the client, at least fifteen, then sort them on the table or floor. The physical sorting draws out distinctions a form misses, and the client can move cards as beliefs change. Photograph the finished ladder and use it to choose the next approach step.

fields.label: Situations we wrote on cards
The bottom three cards
The top three cards
Cards I moved while sorting, and why
The card I will start with
The card I cannot imagine reaching yet

title: Body Neutrality Practice
summary: Daily short statements about what the body did today rather than how it looked.
goal: Move the client's relationship with their body from judgment toward function and use.
duration: Two minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Aim for neutral, not positive; clients who cannot believe their body is beautiful can believe it carried them up the stairs. Keep the statements about doing and feeling. Notice when the client sneaks an appearance comment in and gently redirect. Never mention weight, shape or food in this practice.

fields.label: Three things my body did for me today
One thing it let me feel (warmth, music, a hug, the wind)
A neutral statement about my body, without judgment either way
What my mind wanted to add about how it looks
How I responded to that
The statement I will use tomorrow morning

title: Body Checking Log
summary: Records the mirror checks, pinching, comparing and photo scrutiny that keep body worry alive, and what each one did to mood.
goal: Show the client how checking feeds the worry, and plan a reduction.
body_md: Checking feels like getting information but produces worse mood almost every time; the log makes that visible. Include the quiet forms: reflections in windows, comparing in group photos, clothes tried and discarded. Plan one check to cut in half, not to stop entirely.

fields.label: Date and time
What I checked, and how (mirror, pinch, photo, comparing)
What I was looking for
Mood before and after (0-10)
How long the reassurance lasted, if any
The check I will cut in half next week
What I will do instead in that moment

title: Appearance Assumptions Sheet
summary: Lists the client's rules linking appearance to worth, acceptance or success, and tests each one.
goal: Loosen the beliefs that make appearance carry the whole weight of self-worth.
body_md: Draw out the if-then rules: if I looked different, then people would... Test each against the client's own experience and the people they admire. The goal is to shrink the share of self-worth that appearance holds, which a pie chart of what makes up their worth can show before and after.

fields.label: My rules about appearance (if I looked..., then...)
Where each rule came from
Evidence from my own life for and against it
People I admire, and how much their looks have to do with it
How much of my self-worth appearance holds now (%)
What else I would like it to rest on

title: Body Gratitude Function List
summary: A list of what the client's body has carried them through, by life stage, written as a record rather than a rating.
goal: Build a history of the body as a companion rather than an object under review.
body_md: Move through life stages: childhood play, illness survived, work done, people carried, places reached. The tone is a record, not a pep talk. Clients with a history of harming or overworking their body may find this tender; slow down there. No comments on shape or size anywhere on the sheet.

fields.label: What my body did for me as a child
What it has carried me through
What it lets me do that I would miss
Someone it has held or helped
Something it recovered from
What I would like to thank it for, plainly

title: Media Diet Audit
summary: An inventory of the accounts, shows and images the client consumes, and what each does to how they feel in their body.
goal: Change what the client feeds their body image, since much of it arrives through a screen.
body_md: Go through the phone together. For each account or habit, ask what it does to the client's body feeling in the ten minutes after. Unfollowing is a real intervention and often the fastest one; replace, do not just remove, so the feed is not empty. Repeat in a month.

fields.label: Accounts and shows I see most
How I feel in my body after each (better, worse, nothing)
The ones that leave me comparing
Accounts I will unfollow or mute this week
What I will follow instead (bodies doing things, other interests entirely)
How my feed feels after the change

title: Session Agenda and Priorities Sheet
summary: A short sheet for client and clinician to set the session agenda together.
goal: Use it to open a session with a shared plan instead of guessing where to start.
body_md: Hand this over in the first minute of a session so the client has a hand in shaping it. It works well for clients who tend to bury the thing they most want to talk about until the last five minutes, or who show up without a clear sense of what they need that day. Ranking items by weight, not just listing them, is the part clients skip if you do not prompt for it.

fields.label: What has happened since we last met that you want to make sure we cover?
List up to three things you could talk about today.
Which one matters most right now, and why?
Is there anything you would rather leave for another day?
What would make today feel like it was worth the hour?

title: Family Genogram Sketch
summary: A guided sheet for sketching three generations of family relationships and patterns.
goal: Use it to map family structure, roles and recurring patterns for case formulation.
body_md: Draw the shapes together on a blank page rather than handing over a printed template; the act of building it out loud surfaces detail a form would miss. Ask about closeness, conflict and cutoff between people, not just who is related to whom, and note repeating patterns across generations, such as who tends to caretake or who tends to leave. Keep the focus on structure and pattern, not on assigning blame to any one relative.

fields.label: Who is in your immediate family, and how would you describe each relationship in one word?
Who else has mattered to you growing up, inside or outside the family?
Where do you see closeness in the family? Where do you see distance or conflict?
Are there patterns that seem to repeat across generations, like divorce, addiction or estrangement?
What role do you tend to play in the family, and has that role changed over time?

title: Sleep Habits and Wind-Down Log
summary: A one-week log for tracking bedtime routine, sleep timing and morning alertness.
goal: Use it to spot habits that are keeping sleep light, late or interrupted.
body_md: This is a plain observation log, not a sleep study; the point is to make a week of habits visible rather than relied-on memory. Watch for screens, caffeine timing and inconsistent wake times more than for the number of hours logged. Clients who insist their sleep is fine often find the log tells a different story once they see a week laid out side by side.

fields.label: Monday: bedtime, wake time, and how rested you felt on waking.
Tuesday: bedtime, wake time, and how rested you felt on waking.
Wednesday: bedtime, wake time, and how rested you felt on waking.
Thursday: bedtime, wake time, and how rested you felt on waking.
Friday: bedtime, wake time, and how rested you felt on waking.
Saturday and Sunday: bedtime, wake time, and how rested you felt on waking.
What did the week show you about your wind-down routine?

title: End-of-Therapy Reflection Sheet
summary: A closing worksheet for reviewing progress and planning for life after therapy ends.
goal: Use it to mark what changed, name remaining risks, and plan how to keep gains going.
body_md: Save this for the last session or two rather than handing it out cold; clients often need a nudge to notice change that happened gradually. Naming early warning signs and a plan for them matters as much as celebrating progress, since relapse of old patterns is common and normal after ending care. Leave room for ambivalence about ending; wanting to stop and being nervous about stopping usually coexist.

fields.label: What is different now compared to when you started?
Which skill or idea from our work together do you use the most?
What still feels shaky or unfinished?
What are your early warning signs that things are slipping?
What is your plan if those signs show up?
Who or what can you lean on if you need support after ending here?

title: Weekly Goals and Barriers Tracker
summary: A repeating one-week sheet for setting a small goal and naming what might get in the way.
goal: Use it to build the habit of planning for obstacles before they derail a goal.
body_md: Keep the weekly goal small enough that it is genuinely achievable in a normal week; overreaching is the most common way this tracker fails. The barrier column is the part that does the real work, since naming a likely obstacle in advance makes it far easier to plan around than discovering it mid-week. Review last week's sheet at the start of the next session before starting a new one.

fields.label: This week, what is one goal you want to make progress on?
What could get in the way of that goal this week?
What is your plan if that obstacle shows up?
How will you know by the end of the week whether you made progress?
Looking back, what actually happened?

title: Situation-Thought-Feeling-Behavior Chart
summary: A four-column chart that teaches the basic cognitive model with a client's own example.
goal: Use it to introduce how situations, thoughts, feelings and behavior connect.
body_md: This is the psychoeducation piece before a full thought record, best used the first time a client is introduced to the cognitive model. Walk through one recent, specific moment together rather than asking for a general pattern, since a single concrete example makes the links between the four columns click faster than an abstract explanation. Once a client can fill this in unprompted, they are usually ready for more detailed thought-work tools.

fields.label: Describe one specific recent situation.
What thought went through your mind in that moment?
What feeling came with that thought, and how strong was it, 0 to 10?
What did you do next?
Looking at all four boxes together, what do you notice?

title: Cognitive Distortions Checklist
summary: A plain-language checklist of common unhelpful thinking patterns to spot in daily thoughts.
goal: Use it to build a client's ear for their own recurring thinking patterns.
body_md: Give the client a recent thought and have them check every pattern that seems to fit rather than forcing a single label; several often overlap in one thought. The value is in recognition, not labeling the thought as bad, and a lighter tone here helps, since clients often enjoy naming their own mind's favorite tricks once the shame is taken out of it. Revisit the checklist across sessions to see which patterns show up most.

fields.label: Write down one thought you have had recently that felt sticky or upsetting.
Does it jump to the worst outcome? Check yes or no and explain.
Does it treat a feeling as if it were a fact?
Does it use words like always, never, or everyone?
Does it predict the future as if it were certain?
Which pattern shows up most often for you, based on this and past weeks?

title: Behavior Experiment Design Sheet
summary: A structured sheet for designing a small real-world test of a belief before and after it runs.
goal: Use it to turn a client's prediction into a testable, time-limited experiment.
body_md: The prediction has to be specific and falsifiable, or the experiment will not teach anything; push back gently if a client writes something too vague to be tested. Keep the first experiment small and low-stakes so it is likely to actually happen. The review section at the end matters more than the plan, since it is where the gap between prediction and outcome does the work.

fields.label: What belief or prediction do you want to test?
What specific action will you take to test it?
What do you predict will happen, in detail?
How confident are you in that prediction, 0 to 100?
What actually happened when you tried it?
What does the outcome tell you about the original belief?

title: Thought vs Fact Sorting Card
summary: A short in-session card for sorting a list of statements into thoughts and facts.
goal: Use it to strengthen the basic skill of telling a thought apart from a fact.
body_md: This is a warm-up exercise, useful before deeper cognitive work with a client who tends to treat every thought as automatically true. Mix in a few statements that are genuinely factual along with opinions and predictions, so the sorting is not a trick question. If a client struggles, ask what evidence would prove the statement true in a courtroom sense; that framing often clarifies the line quickly.

fields.label: Write three thoughts you have had this week about yourself, others, or the future.
For each one, mark it as a thought or a fact, and explain your reasoning.
For any you marked as facts, what evidence supports that?
For any you marked as thoughts, how might a friend see it differently?

title: Weekly Automatic Thought Tally
summary: A simple week-long tally of how often a few common automatic thoughts show up.
goal: Use it to track the frequency of unhelpful thoughts over time, not just their content.
body_md: This trades depth for frequency: instead of writing out a full thought record every time, the client makes a quick mark each time a familiar thought shows up. It works well for clients who find full thought records tedious or who need to see change in volume over several weeks rather than in a single entry. Compare tallies week to week rather than judging any single day.

fields.label: List up to three thoughts you want to track this week.
Monday through Wednesday: tally marks for each thought.
Thursday through Saturday: tally marks for each thought.
Sunday: tally marks for each thought.
What changed compared to last week's tally, if you have one?

title: Tug-of-War With the Struggle Monster
summary: A metaphor exercise about dropping the rope in a tug-of-war with a difficult feeling.
goal: Use it to introduce the idea of stopping the struggle instead of winning it.
body_md: Walk the metaphor through slowly: a monster on one end of a rope, the client pulling with all their strength, exhausted and no closer to winning. Ask what happens to the pulling, not the monster, if the client simply drops the rope. This lands best after a client has already described a struggle they keep losing to, so the metaphor maps onto something real rather than staying abstract.

fields.label: What feeling or thought have you been in a tug-of-war with lately?
What does "pulling harder" look like for you in real life?
What has pulling harder actually gotten you?
What would "dropping the rope" look like, practically, this week?
What are you afraid would happen if you dropped it?

title: Sushi Train of Thoughts Practice
summary: A defusion exercise imagining thoughts passing by on a conveyor belt to be watched, not grabbed.
goal: Use it to practice noticing thoughts without acting on every one that passes.
body_md: Guide the client to picture each thought as a small plate going past on a conveyor belt: some plates look tempting, some look unpleasant, and the instruction either way is to watch rather than grab. This is easiest to teach after a short stretch of quiet in the room, so the thoughts have something to arrive against. Some clients prefer the plates on a treadmill; adjust the image to whatever sticks for them.

fields.label: Sit quietly for two minutes and notice the thoughts that pass through your mind.
What did you notice yourself wanting to grab onto?
What happened when you let a thought pass without grabbing it?
How is this different from your usual way of relating to thoughts?

title: Values vs Goals Sorting Sheet
summary: A worksheet that separates a client's values, which are directions, from their goals, which are destinations.
goal: Use it to clarify the difference between an ongoing direction and a finishable target.
body_md: Clients often confuse the two, listing goals as values or treating values as things to finish and check off. Use the compass-versus-destination framing: a value like being a caring friend never gets "completed," while a goal like calling a friend today does. This sheet works well as a bridge into any values-based planning that follows, since it clears up the confusion before it derails later work.

fields.label: List three things that matter to you, without worrying yet whether they are values or goals.
For each one, ask: can this ever be finished and checked off? If yes, it is likely a goal.
Sort your list into values and goals based on that question.
Pick one value. What is one small goal this week that would move you in that direction?

title: Committed Action Weekly Planner
summary: A repeating weekly sheet for planning one values-based action and reviewing how it went.
goal: Use it to build a habit of small, regular action in line with a client's stated values.
body_md: This is the follow-through piece after values work: a small planned action, tied explicitly to a named value, reviewed the next week. Keep the action modest and specific rather than aspirational, since the point is building a pattern of action over months, not a single impressive week. When an action does not happen, treat it as information about barriers rather than a failure to correct with more willpower.

fields.label: Which value does this week's action connect to?
What specific action will you take, and when?
What might get in the way?
Did the action happen? What actually occurred?
What did you learn for next week's plan?

title: Present Moment Senses Anchor
summary: A brief five-senses exercise for making contact with the present moment in session.
goal: Use it to practice shifting attention from thought to direct present-moment experience.
body_md: Use this as a short reset at any point a client seems pulled entirely into thought, worry or story. Go slowly through each sense rather than rushing to the next, since the value is in dwelling in direct experience, not completing a checklist. This is a present-moment contact exercise rather than a crisis tool, though the two families of skill can look similar in practice.

fields.label: Name three things you can see right now.
Name two things you can hear right now.
Name one thing you can feel physically right now, like your feet on the floor.
What shifted, if anything, after doing this?

title: What and How Mindfulness Skills Card
summary: A reference card teaching the DBT what skills and how skills of mindfulness practice.
goal: Use it to teach observing, describing and participating, done nonjudgmentally and one thing at a time.
body_md: Introduce the what skills, observe, describe, and participate, as three things a client can do with attention, then the how skills, nonjudgmentally, one-mindfully, and effectively, as the manner of doing them. A short in-session practice, like eating a raisin slowly or listening to one sound fully, makes the six skills land better than explaining them in the abstract. Return to this card whenever a client's mindfulness practice needs a refresher.

fields.label: Pick one small activity, like drinking water or walking down a hallway.
Practice it while observing, describing to yourself, and fully participating.
Practice it again while staying nonjudgmental, one-mindful, and effective.
What was different about doing it this way?

title: Emotion Vulnerability Factors Log
summary: A daily log tracking the physical and situational factors that make emotions harder to regulate.
goal: Use it to spot the sleep, food, illness and stress factors that raise a client's emotional baseline.
body_md: This is a precursor to full emotion regulation work: before addressing a reaction to a specific event, it helps to know whether a client was already running on empty. Track the same handful of factors daily, sleep, meals, physical illness, and substance use, alongside the day's hardest emotional moment. Patterns usually appear within a week, and clients are often surprised how much a skipped meal or short night explains.

fields.label: How many hours did you sleep last night?
Did you eat regular meals today? Yes, no, or partly.
Were you dealing with any physical illness or pain today?
What was the hardest emotional moment of your day?
Looking at the whole week, which factor seems to matter most for you?

title: Turning the Mind Practice
summary: A short practice for choosing acceptance of a hard reality, moment by moment, without pretending to like it.
goal: Use it to practice the repeated choice to accept a fact rather than fight it.
body_md: Explain that turning the mind is a repeated choice, like standing at a fork in the road and turning toward acceptance each time the mind wanders back toward fighting reality, not a single decision made once. It does not require agreeing with or liking the situation, only ceasing the fight against the fact that it is happening. Clients often need to hear that turning the mind may need to happen dozens of times about the same fact before it feels steady.

fields.label: What is a hard reality you find yourself fighting against right now?
What does "fighting it" look like for you, in thoughts or actions?
Practice turning your mind toward accepting the fact, just for this moment. What happened?
What would change if you kept choosing this, even without liking it?

title: Willingness vs Willfulness Check
summary: A short check-in for noticing when a client has shifted from willingness into willfulness.
goal: Use it to help a client recognize digging in against reality versus working with it.
body_md: Willfulness looks like refusing to do what is needed, giving up, or insisting on being right even when it costs more than it gains; willingness looks like doing what the moment calls for, even reluctantly. Use a recent example rather than a hypothetical one, and avoid moralizing the willful moment, since clients usually already know it did not serve them. The goal is recognition in the moment, which takes repeated practice to build.

fields.label: Describe a recent situation where things did not go the way you wanted.
Looking back, did you respond with willingness or willfulness?
What signs tell you which one it was?
What would a willing response have looked like instead?

title: Self-Validation Practice Card
summary: A short prompt card for practicing validating one's own emotional reaction before problem-solving it.
goal: Use it to build the habit of validating a reaction before trying to change or fix it.
body_md: Many clients move straight to fixing or judging an emotional reaction without ever acknowledging that it made sense given the situation; this card slows that down. Model the language out loud first, since self-validation can feel foreign or self-indulgent to clients who were taught to dismiss their own reactions. Note that validating the reaction is separate from agreeing the resulting action was the best choice.

fields.label: What emotional reaction are you being hard on yourself about?
Given the situation, how does that reaction make sense?
Write one sentence validating the reaction, starting with "It makes sense that..."
Now that it is validated, is there anything you still want to work on or change?

title: Pursue-Withdraw Cycle Map
summary: A worksheet for mapping the pursue-and-withdraw pattern a couple falls into during conflict.
goal: Use it to help both partners see the cycle as the shared problem, not the other person.
body_md: Draw the cycle as a loop on paper with both partners present: one partner's pursuit triggers the other's withdrawal, and that withdrawal triggers more pursuit, round and round. The reframe that matters most is naming the cycle itself as the enemy, not either partner's behavior in isolation. Expect some resistance to this framing at first, since each partner usually arrives certain the other one started it.

fields.label: Partner A: when do you notice yourself pursuing, and what does it look like?
Partner B: when do you notice yourself withdrawing, and what does it look like?
What usually triggers the first move in the cycle?
What does each of you feel underneath the pursuing or withdrawing?
What would help you both step out of the cycle earlier next time?

title: Attachment Injury Timeline
summary: A guided sheet for identifying a specific past moment that damaged trust between partners.
goal: Use it to name a wounding moment clearly enough to work on repairing it.
body_md: An attachment injury is a specific moment, not a general pattern, often a time one partner needed the other and felt abandoned or betrayed in a way that still colors the relationship. Slow the pace here; this exercise can bring up strong feelings, and rushing to resolution before both partners feel heard tends to backfire. The goal of this sheet is naming the injury clearly, not resolving it in one sitting.

fields.label: Partner A: is there a specific moment that still feels unresolved between you? Describe it.
What did you need in that moment that you did not get?
Partner B: what is it like to hear this moment described?
What would help Partner A feel that moment is being taken seriously now?

title: Forgiveness Readiness Scale
summary: A short scale for each partner to privately rate where they stand on working toward forgiveness.
goal: Use it to open an honest conversation about readiness without pressuring either partner.
body_md: Have each partner fill this out separately before comparing, since social pressure to say "I forgive you" too soon can bury real ambivalence. A low number is useful information, not a failure, and naming what is missing gives the couple something concrete to work toward rather than a vague expectation of moving on. Revisit the scale over weeks rather than expecting it to shift in one conversation.

fields.label: On a scale of 0 to 10, where do you feel you are in working toward forgiveness?
What would need to happen for that number to move up?
What are you afraid would happen if you forgave too soon?
What do you need from your partner right now, regardless of where the number sits?

title: Household Team Meeting Agenda
summary: A short weekly agenda template for a couple to run their household like a working team.
goal: Use it to keep logistics conversations short, regular and separate from emotional processing time.
body_md: Logistics conversations that happen only when something has gone wrong tend to turn into conflict; a standing short meeting for scheduling and chores takes that pressure off other conversations. Keep this meeting strictly practical, and if deeper relationship issues come up, note them for another time rather than letting the agenda balloon. Consistency matters more than length here.

fields.label: What is on the calendar this week that needs coordinating?
What household tasks need to be divided or caught up on?
Is anything feeling unfair in the current division of tasks?
One thing to appreciate about how the other partner handled something this week.

title: Post-Conflict Debrief Worksheet
summary: A structured sheet for reviewing a past argument together once both partners have cooled down.
goal: Use it to extract what a conflict revealed, once emotions have settled enough to look at it.
body_md: Wait until well after the argument has cooled, ideally a day later, rather than debriefing while either partner is still flooded. The point is not re-litigating who was right, but noticing what each person needed underneath the fight and what each contributed to how it escalated. Coach both partners to speak about their own part before commenting on the other's.

fields.label: Partner A: what did you need in that moment that you did not ask for directly?
Partner A: what did you do that made things harder?
Partner B: what did you need in that moment that you did not ask for directly?
Partner B: what did you do that made things harder?
What would you both do differently if a similar moment came up again?

title: All About Me Poster Craft
summary: A first-sessions poster where a child draws and writes about themselves to build rapport.
goal: Use it to get to know a child and build comfort in the therapy space.
body_md: This works best in the first session or two, before diving into any harder material, and gives a quieter child something concrete to do with their hands while talking. A parent can help gather photos or favorite items ahead of time if the clinician wants to send a note home first. Keep the tone light and curious; this is rapport-building, not assessment.

fields.label: Draw a picture of yourself in the middle of the page.
Write or draw three things you like to do.
Write or draw the people and pets in your life.
Write or draw one thing you are really good at.
Write or draw one thing you hope happens by coming here.

title: Calm Down Corner Design Craft
summary: A craft where a child designs a calm-down space for home, with the parent helping set it up.
goal: Use it to give a child ownership over a physical space for settling down.
body_md: Have the child draw or describe their ideal calm corner first, then talk with the parent about what is realistic to set up at home, even if it is just a cushion in a corner. Emphasize that this is a place to go to feel better, never a punishment or a time-out spot, and the child should be able to choose to use it. Check back in a few sessions later on whether the corner got built and used.

fields.label: Draw or describe a cozy, calm spot you would want in your home.
What would you want to have there, like pillows, books, or toys?
What could you do there when you feel upset?
Parent: where in the home could a space like this actually go?

title: Session Rules Poster Craft
summary: A craft where a child helps create and decorate the ground rules for their therapy sessions.
goal: Use it to give a child a sense of ownership and predictability in the therapy space.
body_md: Keep the list short, three to five rules the child helps phrase in their own words, covering things like respect, safety, and what happens with anything they share. This is also a natural moment to explain confidentiality and its limits in plain, age-appropriate language the child can understand and refer back to. Post the finished poster somewhere visible in future sessions.

fields.label: What is one rule that would help our time together feel safe?
What is one rule about being kind to each other?
Decorate the poster with colors or pictures.
Is there anything you are curious or nervous about, about coming here?

title: My Body Owner's Manual Craft
summary: A craft where a child describes what their body needs to feel good, like sleep, movement and rest.
goal: Use it to build a child's awareness of their own basic care needs.
body_md: Frame this around function and care, not appearance: what the body needs to have energy, feel calm, and get through the day well. This works well alongside sleep or routine work with a parent present to help fill in realistic details. Keep language strictly about needs like rest, movement, and food timing, never about size, weight or how the body looks.

fields.label: Draw an outline of your body and label parts that help you move, think, or rest.
What helps your body feel rested?
What helps your body feel calm when it is upset?
What does your body need more of, based on a normal week?

title: Kindness Tracker Chart Craft
summary: A craft chart where a child tracks small acts of kindness given and received over a week.
goal: Use it to build a child's awareness of prosocial behavior in both directions.
body_md: Have the child decorate the chart first, then add a sticker or mark each time they notice an act of kindness, either one they did or one someone did for them. This works well for children building social skills or self-esteem, since it broadens attention beyond only moments that went wrong. Review the chart together the following week rather than checking in daily.

fields.label: Decorate your kindness chart with colors or stickers.
Monday and Tuesday: write or draw one kind thing you did or noticed.
Wednesday and Thursday: write or draw one kind thing you did or noticed.
Friday through Sunday: write or draw one kind thing you did or noticed.
What did you notice about doing this for a week?

title: Group Trust Web Game
summary: A group game where a ball of yarn is passed around while sharing, building a visible web of connection.
goal: Use it to build group cohesion and a felt sense of connection early in group work.
body_md: Sitting or standing in a circle, one person holds the end of a ball of yarn, shares something brief, then tosses the ball to someone else while keeping hold of the string, building a web across the group. Keep the prompts light for a first group, such as a favorite place or something they are looking forward to, and save deeper prompts for a group that has already met a few times. Debrief by pointing out how the web looks messy but holds together, much like the group.

fields.label: Prompt for the round: share one thing about yourself as you toss the yarn.
What did it feel like to see the web build across the group?
What does the web remind you of about how this group works together?
What is one thing you want this group to know about you going forward?

title: Session Check-In Dice Game
summary: A game where rolling a die matches a number to a check-in prompt to open the session.
goal: Use it to make opening check-ins more engaging for clients who find them repetitive.
body_md: Number six prompts one through six and let the client roll to see which they answer; this small element of chance makes an otherwise routine check-in feel less like a chore. It works well at the start of nearly any session and can be reused indefinitely by simply rewriting the prompt list from time to time. In a group, pass the die around so each member answers a different roll.

fields.label: Roll 1: how has your week been, in one word?
Roll 2: what is something that went well recently?
Roll 3: what has been hard lately?
Roll 4: what do you want to make sure we talk about today?
Roll 5: what is your energy level right now, 1 to 10?
Roll 6: is there anything you are avoiding bringing up?

title: Feelings Face Match-Up Game
summary: A memory-style matching game pairing feeling faces with situations that could cause them.
goal: Use it to build a client's vocabulary for naming emotions tied to situations.
body_md: Lay out two sets of face-down cards, one with feeling faces and one with short situations, and take turns flipping two at a time looking for a match. There is often more than one reasonable match for a situation card, which is a useful discussion point rather than a problem with the game. This works well for younger clients still building emotional vocabulary, and for groups as a shared warm-up.

fields.label: Write or draw six different feeling faces on separate cards.
Write six short situations that could cause a feeling, on separate cards.
Play the matching game, explaining your reasoning for each match.
Was there a situation that could match more than one feeling? Which ones?

title: Common Ground Mingle Bingo
summary: A group mingling game where members find others who share an experience listed on their bingo card.
goal: Use it to build early connection in a group by surfacing shared experiences.
body_md: Fill a bingo grid with light, low-pressure prompts, such as "has a pet" or "is working on patience," and have members mingle to find someone matching each square and sign it. This works best in the first few sessions of a group when members are still learning each other's names and finding common ground lowers early anxiety. Debrief by asking what surprised them about what they shared with others.

fields.label: Fill in your bingo card with prompts, or use the ones provided.
Mingle and find someone matching each square; have them sign it.
What did you learn about someone you did not know before?
What was it like to find something in common with the group?

title: Would You Rather: Values Edition
summary: A discussion game using paired values-based choices to explore what a client prioritizes.
goal: Use it to surface a client's values through playful, low-stakes forced choices.
body_md: Read out a series of would-you-rather pairs built around values rather than trivia, such as more free time or more recognition at work, and have the client choose and explain. The explanation matters more than the choice itself, since it is where the underlying value gets named. In a group, let members compare answers, which often sparks discussion about how differently people weigh the same trade-off.

fields.label: Would you rather have more time or more money? Why?
Would you rather be known for kindness or for achievement? Why?
Would you rather have one close friend or many acquaintances? Why?
Would you rather take a safe path or a risky one toward a dream? Why?
Looking at your answers, what do they say about what you value?

title: Trauma Timeline of Safety and Support
summary: A timeline worksheet marking moments of safety and support across a client's life.
goal: Use it to build a resource of remembered safety without revisiting traumatic detail.
body_md: Keep this focused strictly on safety and support, people, places, and moments that felt protective, never on the traumatic events themselves. Clients sometimes default to narrating what went wrong; gently redirect back to what and who kept them steady. The finished timeline becomes a resource to return to during grounding work.

fields.label: Mark a moment early in life when you felt safe or supported.
Mark a person who has been steady for you, at any point.
Mark a more recent moment of safety or support.
Which of these could you lean on more right now?

title: Meaning and Growth Reflection After Trauma
summary: A reflection worksheet on strengths and changes a client notices in themselves since a hard period.
goal: Use it to notice growth and strength without needing to revisit traumatic detail.
body_md: This stays entirely present-focused: what a client notices about themselves now, not an account of what happened. Some clients will not find growth to name yet, and that is a fine answer; do not push for positivity before it is genuine. Use it in the later, more stable stretch of work, not early on.

fields.label: What is something you know about your own strength now that you did not before?
Has anything in your relationships or priorities shifted?
What would you tell someone else going through something hard?
What does this tell you about where you are today?

title: Window Widening Skills Card
summary: A reference card of skills matched to whether a client is under- or over-aroused after activation.
goal: Use it to match a specific skill to whether the body is flooded or shut down.
body_md: Pair this with any existing window-of-tolerance map: once a client can name whether they are above, below, or inside the window, this card gives them a specific next step for each zone, movement and cold water for shutdown, slow breath and grounding for flooding. Practice each skill in session before relying on the card in a hard moment.

fields.label: When you feel shut down or numb, which skill from the card will you try?
When you feel flooded or panicked, which skill from the card will you try?
What tells your body it has moved back inside the window?
Which skill felt most doable when you tried it this week?

title: Rebuilding Physical Closeness Pace Conversation
summary: A paced conversation guide for a couple navigating physical closeness after trauma.
goal: Use it to help both partners agree on pace and cues for physical closeness.
body_md: Keep this conversation about pace, comfort, and signals, never a request to explain or justify why closeness feels hard right now. The partner without trauma history often needs coaching that slowing down is not rejection. Agree on a clear, low-stakes way to pause in the moment that both partners will actually use.

fields.label: What kinds of closeness currently feel comfortable?
What signal will you use if you need to pause?
Partner: how can you respond supportively if that signal comes up?
What would feel like a good, manageable next step for you both?

title: My Safety Plan Coloring Page
summary: A coloring page where a child draws people, places and things that help them feel safe.
goal: Use it to give a child a visible, personal reminder of safety and support.
body_md: Keep this focused on safety, comfort and helpers, never on retelling what happened; a child's job here is to color and point, not narrate. If a child discloses anything during this activity, pause the craft and follow your state's mandatory reporting duties before continuing. Send the finished page home with the parent as a visual reminder.

fields.label: Color a picture of a safe place.
Draw or write the names of grown-ups who help you feel safe.
Draw something that helps your body feel calm.
Who could you go to if you felt scared or unsafe?

title: Worry Outcome Prediction Log
summary: A log for predicting a worry's outcome in advance, then checking it against what actually happened.
goal: Use it to build evidence that most predicted worries do not play out as feared.
body_md: Have the client log a worry and their predicted outcome before the event, then return to the same entry afterward with what actually happened. The pattern across several entries tends to do more convincing than any single one. Review the log together rather than leaving the insight for the client to find alone.

fields.label: What are you worried will happen?
How likely does it feel right now, 0 to 100?
What actually happened afterward?
How did the prediction compare to reality?

title: Anxiety Fuel Sources Worksheet
summary: A worksheet identifying the daily habits, caffeine, sleep and avoidance patterns that feed anxiety.
goal: Use it to map the everyday factors that raise or lower a client's baseline anxiety.
body_md: This widens the lens beyond a single worry to the daily habits quietly raising baseline anxiety, caffeine, screen use before bed, and avoidance that shrinks a client's world over time. Clients are often surprised how many small factors stack up. Pick one or two to adjust rather than overhauling everything at once.

fields.label: What in your daily routine tends to raise your anxiety?
What tends to lower it, even briefly?
What are you currently avoiding because of anxiety?
Which one factor would you like to adjust first?

title: Anxious Mind as Overprotective Guard Metaphor
summary: A metaphor exercise framing anxious thoughts as an overprotective guard doing its job too well.
goal: Use it to relate to anxious thoughts with less struggle by seeing their protective intent.
body_md: Introduce the image of an overeager guard who sounds the alarm for everything, even harmless things, because it takes its job of protecting the client seriously. The move is not to fire the guard but to thank it and decide for oneself whether the alarm is worth acting on. This tends to soften the fight clients have with their own anxious mind.

fields.label: What does your anxious "guard" tend to warn you about most?
What is it trying to protect you from?
What would it look like to thank the guard without obeying every alarm?
What could you do instead, values in hand?

title: Anxiety Opposite Action Ladder
summary: A stepped ladder for practicing opposite action against anxiety-driven avoidance.
goal: Use it to plan graduated steps of approaching what anxiety says to avoid.
body_md: Build the ladder together, ranking steps from least to most uncomfortable, and confirm the emotion does not fit the actual facts of the situation before assigning opposite action. Start on a low rung and build confidence before moving up. Review what happened after each attempted step, not just whether it was completed.

fields.label: What is anxiety telling you to avoid?
List three to five steps from easiest to hardest toward approaching it.
Which step will you try this week?
What happened when you tried it?

title: Worry Whack-a-Mole Game
summary: A quick-response game where players respond to popped-up worries with a coping skill before time runs out.
goal: Use it to practice quick access to coping skills for common worries in a playful format.
body_md: Write common worries on small cards or cups; a player "pops up" a worry and has a short time limit to name a coping skill that fits before the next one appears. Keep the pace brisk and the tone playful, since the point is building quick, almost reflexive access to skills. Debrief by asking which skills came fastest and which felt shakier.

fields.label: Write five common worries on separate cards or cups.
For each one popped, name a coping skill within ten seconds.
Which skill came to mind fastest?
Which worry was hardest to respond to quickly?

title: Energy Budget Worksheet
summary: A worksheet for planning a day's limited energy across tasks that drain and tasks that restore.
goal: Use it to plan a realistic day when energy is low rather than overcommitting.
body_md: Treat energy like a limited daily budget rather than an unlimited resource, and have the client list planned tasks alongside their rough energy cost. Low mood often comes with a habit of overcommitting and then feeling like a failure; this worksheet makes the math visible in advance. Build in at least one restoring item, not only obligations.

fields.label: List what you need or want to do today.
Next to each, estimate how much energy it will take, low, medium or high.
What is one thing today that will restore energy rather than spend it?
Does today's list actually fit your energy budget? What would you cut?

title: Self-Criticism to Self-Coaching Rewrite
summary: A worksheet rewriting harsh self-critical thoughts into the voice of a firm but fair coach.
goal: Use it to shift a client's inner voice from punishing to firm and workable.
body_md: A coach voice is firm and honest, unlike a purely soft self-compassion voice some clients resist, so it can be an easier bridge for clients who find kindness toward themselves hard to accept. Have the client write the harsh thought first, then rewrite it as something a good coach would actually say, direct but not cruel. Practice saying the rewritten version out loud.

fields.label: Write a self-critical thought you have had recently.
What would a firm, fair coach say instead, in that same situation?
What is the difference in how each version lands?
Which version would help you actually take the next step?

title: Values Beneath the Low Mood Practice
summary: An exercise identifying what a client still cares about even when motivation is absent.
goal: Use it to locate values that can guide action even without feeling motivated first.
body_md: Depression often removes the feeling of wanting before it removes what a client actually values, so this exercise separates the two. Ask what would still matter even if the low mood never lifted, which tends to surface values obscured by the absence of motivation. Use the answer to choose one small action, not a full life overhaul.

fields.label: Even without motivation, what still feels like it matters to you?
What has low mood made harder to act on, even though it still matters?
What is one small action, values in hand, you could take today?
What got in the way the last time you tried something like this?

title: Behavioral Activation Barrier Troubleshoot
summary: A troubleshooting sheet for identifying why a planned activity did not happen and adjusting the plan.
goal: Use it to problem-solve stalled behavioral activation plans rather than abandoning them.
body_md: When a planned activity does not happen, treat it as a troubleshooting problem rather than a personal failure. Common barriers include the task being too large, too vague, or scheduled at low-energy times; naming the specific barrier makes the next attempt more realistic. Shrink the task until it feels almost too easy before trying again.

fields.label: What activity did you plan that did not happen?
What got in the way?
How could the task be made smaller or easier?
When will you try again, and what will be different?

title: Supporting a Partner's Low Mood Without Rescuing
summary: A conversation guide for a partner to offer support without over-functioning or fixing.
goal: Use it to help a supporting partner find a sustainable middle ground between helping and rescuing.
body_md: Supporting partners often swing between overfunctioning, taking over everything, and burning out or resenting it. This conversation names specific tasks the depressed partner can still manage versus ones that genuinely need support, so help has boundaries. Check in on the supporting partner's own needs too, since caregiver strain is common and worth naming.

fields.label: Partner with low mood: what do you want help with right now?
What do you want to keep doing yourself, even if it is hard?
Supporting partner: what is sustainable for you to offer right now?
What does the supporting partner need for themselves?

title: Task Friction Audit Worksheet
summary: A worksheet identifying the small frictions that make starting a task harder than it needs to be.
goal: Use it to find and remove small obstacles that block task initiation.
body_md: Friction is often small and fixable: a task requiring three steps before it can even start, a missing supply, an unclear first move. Walk through a stuck task in detail and look for the exact point it stalls rather than assuming the problem is motivation. Reducing friction by even one step often unsticks a task that willpower alone could not.

fields.label: What task have you been avoiding starting?
What has to happen before you can even begin?
Where exactly does it usually stall?
What is one way to reduce the friction at that point?

title: Time Blindness Reality Check Log
summary: A log comparing estimated versus actual time spent on tasks to build a more accurate internal clock.
goal: Use it to build more accurate time estimates by tracking the gap over time.
body_md: Have the client estimate how long a task will take before starting, then log the actual time it took. The gap is usually informative rather than embarrassing, and naming it as a real perceptual difference, not laziness, tends to reduce shame. Use the pattern to build in buffer time for future planning.

fields.label: What task are you about to start?
How long do you estimate it will take?
How long did it actually take?
What does the pattern across several tasks tell you?

title: Rejection Sensitivity Check Card
summary: A short card for checking whether a perceived criticism is as big as it feels in the moment.
goal: Use it to slow down and check facts before reacting to a felt slight.
body_md: Many clients with ADHD describe a sharp, outsized sting from perceived criticism or rejection. This card is a quick facts-check to use in the moment: what exactly was said, how big does it feel, and what would checking the facts show. It will not remove the sting entirely, but it can slow the urge to react before checking.

fields.label: What was said or happened that felt like a criticism or rejection?
How big does it feel right now, 0 to 10?
What do the actual facts of the situation suggest?
What is a response that fits the facts rather than the feeling?

title: Focus Fidget Toolkit Build
summary: A craft where a child builds a small kit of fidget and focus tools to keep at their desk.
goal: Use it to give a child hands-on tools that support focus, chosen and built by them.
body_md: Let the child choose from a few simple options, a stress ball, a textured strip, a doodle pad, and build or decorate their own version rather than handing over a premade kit. A parent can help gather materials and keep the kit stocked at home or school. Frame fidgeting as something that can help focus, not something to be stopped.

fields.label: Which fidget tools do you want to build or decorate?
Where will you keep your kit?
When during the day might you use it?
Parent: where else might a kit like this help, like homework time?

title: Beat the Distraction Relay Game
summary: A relay game practicing refocusing after a planted distraction interrupts a simple task.
goal: Use it to practice noticing distraction and returning to task in a low-stakes, playful way.
body_md: Give players a simple repetitive task, like sorting cards, and plant a distraction partway through, a noise, a question, a funny prop. The goal is to notice the distraction and return to the task, timed for fun rather than judged. Debrief on what helped them return fastest, since that becomes a transferable skill.

fields.label: What was the task you were sorting or building?
What was the distraction that popped up?
How quickly did you notice you had gotten distracted?
What helped you get back to the task?

title: Substance Use Function Map
summary: A worksheet mapping what function substance use currently serves in a client's life.
goal: Use it to identify what need substance use is meeting so it can be met another way.
body_md: Substance use nearly always serves a function, relief, connection, numbing, energy, even when it also causes harm. Naming the function honestly, without a client feeling judged for it, opens the door to finding another way to meet the same need. Keep language centered on substance use and urges, never on labeling the client.

fields.label: What does substance use currently help you feel, avoid, or get through?
When is the urge to use strongest?
What need is being met in those moments?
What else, even partially, could meet that same need?

title: Urge Timeline and Peak Tracker
summary: A tracker charting how an urge rises, peaks and fades over time on a given day.
goal: Use it to build confidence that urges pass on their own within a limited window.
body_md: Have the client rate the urge every ten to fifteen minutes once it starts, plotting a rough curve. Most urges peak and fall within twenty to forty-five minutes, and seeing that shape on paper builds real confidence that riding it out is possible. Compare several tracked urges to build a pattern the client can trust.

fields.label: What time did the urge start, and what triggered it?
Rate the urge every ten to fifteen minutes, 0 to 10.
What was the highest point it reached?
How long did it take to noticeably drop?

title: Values and Sobriety Compass
summary: A worksheet connecting a client's stated values to the daily choice around substance use.
goal: Use it to link the choice to use or not use back to what a client cares about most.
body_md: Rather than framing every choice around willpower, this worksheet connects the daily decision to a client's own stated values, relationships, health, work, parenting, whatever matters most to them. The urge to use rarely disappears from values work alone, but it gives the client something to weigh the urge against. Revisit the compass often, since values can shift over the course of recovery.

fields.label: What matters most to you right now, in this season of life?
How does substance use help or hurt that?
What would moving toward that value look like today?
What might get in the way, and how could you handle it?

title: Urge Riding Skills Card
summary: A reference card of distress tolerance skills matched to different intensities of urge.
goal: Use it to match a specific skill to how strong an urge currently feels.
body_md: Sort skills by intensity, a quick distraction for a mild urge, TIPP or intense sensation for a strong one, so a client is not left guessing what might help in the moment. Practice each skill in session before relying on the card during a real urge. Update the card together as the client learns what actually works for them.

fields.label: What skill works for a mild urge, around 3 out of 10?
What skill works for a moderate urge, around 6 out of 10?
What skill works for an intense urge, 8 or higher?
Which skill have you actually used, and how did it go?

title: Support Without Monitoring Conversation
summary: A conversation guide helping a couple find support that does not slide into surveillance.
goal: Use it to help partners agree on support that feels helpful rather than policed.
body_md: A partner supporting someone working on substance use often defaults to checking up, which can breed resentment on both sides even when it comes from care. This conversation names specific, agreed forms of support, checking in at certain times, being available for a call, versus monitoring that was never asked for. Revisit the agreement as trust rebuilds.

fields.label: Partner in recovery: what kind of support actually helps you?
What starts to feel like monitoring instead of support?
Supporting partner: what do you need to feel less anxious?
What specific agreement can you both commit to this week?

title: Anger Cost Ledger
summary: A worksheet tallying what recent angry reactions have cost against what staying calm might gain.
goal: Use it to weigh the real costs of reactive anger against the benefits of a paused response.
body_md: List a handful of recent angry reactions alongside their actual cost, a damaged relationship, lost time, regret, and set that against what a paused response might have gained. This is not about suppressing anger, which is a valid signal, but about the reaction that follows it. Clients often underestimate the cumulative cost until it is written down.

fields.label: Describe a recent moment you reacted in anger.
