What did that reaction cost you or someone else?
What might a paused, chosen response have looked like?
What might that have gained instead?

title: Anger Trigger Thought Chain
summary: A chain worksheet tracing the thought that turns an irritation into full anger.
goal: Use it to find the specific thought that escalates a minor irritation into anger.
body_md: Anger usually has an appraisal underneath it, often about unfairness or disrespect, that turns an irritation into a full reaction. Trace the chain from trigger to thought to intensity, and look for the exact thought that does the escalating. Testing that specific thought, rather than the anger itself, is usually where change happens.

fields.label: What was the triggering situation?
What thought went through your mind right after?
How did that thought change the intensity of your anger?
Is there another way to read the situation?

title: Anger Early Exit Plan
summary: A plan for exiting a heated moment early, before anger reaches a point of no return.
goal: Use it to build a concrete, rehearsed plan for stepping away before anger peaks.
body_md: The exit has to be planned and specific, a phrase to say, a place to go, a return time, or it tends to get skipped in the moment. Rehearse the exact wording out loud in session, since an awkward or vague exit line is one reason clients avoid using it. Agree with anyone affected, like a partner or family, that this plan exists ahead of time.

fields.label: What is your early warning sign that anger is building?
What exact phrase will you use to exit the moment?
Where will you go, and for how long?
What will you do while you are away to cool down?

title: Repair After an Angry Moment Conversation
summary: A guided conversation for repairing with a partner after an angry outburst.
goal: Use it to structure a genuine repair after anger has affected a partner.
body_md: A repair needs to name the specific behavior, not just say sorry in general, and it needs to include what will be different next time. The partner on the receiving end also needs space to say what the moment was like for them without being rushed past. Avoid re-litigating who was right; that is a separate conversation from repair.

fields.label: What specifically happened that you want to repair?
What was that like for your partner?
What will you do differently next time you feel that angry?
What does your partner need to feel repair has actually happened?

title: Anger Volcano Craft
summary: A craft where a child builds a paper volcano showing the buildup from calm to eruption.
goal: Use it to help a child see anger building in stages rather than arriving all at once.
body_md: Build the volcano in layers, from calm at the base to eruption at the top, and have the child mark body clues at each layer, like a hot face or tight fists. The goal is catching anger lower on the volcano, where it is easier to manage, rather than only after it erupts. A parent can help the child notice their own layers at home.

fields.label: Color the bottom of the volcano: what does calm feel like in your body?
Color the middle: what does your body feel like when anger is building?
Color the top: what happens when anger erupts?
What could help you at the middle layer, before the top?

title: Compulsion Cost-Benefit Ledger
summary: A worksheet weighing the short-term relief of a compulsion against its longer-term cost.
goal: Use it to make the trade-off of a compulsion visible over both short and long timeframes.
body_md: Compulsions offer real short-term relief, which is exactly why they persist; naming that honestly, rather than dismissing it, builds trust. Then widen the timeframe to the longer-term cost, time lost, life narrowed, relief that never lasts. Seeing both columns side by side tends to shift motivation more than being told the compulsion is unhelpful.

fields.label: Name one compulsion you do regularly.
What relief does it give you in the short term?
What has it cost you over weeks or months?
Looking at both, what do you notice?

title: Intrusive Thought Ownership Check
summary: A worksheet separating the content of an intrusive thought from what it says about the client.
goal: Use it to challenge the belief that having a thought means something about the client's character.
body_md: A core piece of OCD work is separating a thought's content from its meaning: having an intrusive thought does not mean a client wants it, endorses it, or is likely to act on it. Walk through the evidence for and against the thought meaning something about their character, and note how everyone has unwanted thoughts pass through their mind.

fields.label: What intrusive thought has been bothering you?
What does it seem to say about you, at first glance?
What evidence actually supports that conclusion?
What is a more accurate way to understand having this thought?

title: Certainty Chasing Defusion Practice
summary: A defusion exercise for noticing the mind's demand for certainty before it can rest.
goal: Use it to build a different relationship with the mind's demand for full certainty.
body_md: Name the pattern out loud: the mind insists on total certainty before it will allow relief, and OCD is expert at manufacturing doubt no amount of checking can fully satisfy. Practice noticing the demand for certainty as just another thought passing through, rather than a rule to obey. This pairs well with any existing uncertainty tolerance work.

fields.label: What does your mind demand certainty about most often?
What has trying to reach full certainty actually gotten you?
Practice naming the thought: "My mind is demanding certainty again." What shifts?
What could you do instead of chasing certainty, right now?

title: Ritual Postponement Ladder
summary: A stepped plan for gradually increasing how long a compulsion is postponed before it can happen.
goal: Use it to build tolerance for delay through a graduated, planned sequence.
body_md: Start with a delay short enough to actually succeed at, even five minutes, and build the interval up gradually rather than jumping to full resistance. Pair the wait with a distress tolerance skill from the client's existing toolkit. Track each attempt so progress across the ladder is visible over time.

fields.label: Which compulsion are you working on postponing?
What is your current, doable delay time?
What skill will you use while you wait?
How did the wait go? Are you ready to increase the delay?

title: Worry Bug Feeding Chart
summary: A chart where a child tracks times they did not feed their "worry bug" with a ritual.
goal: Use it to give a child a visual, encouraging tally of resisting a ritual.
body_md: Pair this with an externalizing name the child already uses for their OCD, like a worry bug or bossy brain. Each time the child notices an urge and does not feed it, they add a mark or sticker, building a visible record of successes rather than dwelling on the times it did not work. Celebrate small counts; this is genuinely hard for a child to do.

fields.label: Draw or name your worry bug.
Each day, mark how many times you did not feed it.
What helped you not feed it?
What do you want to tell your worry bug at the end of the week?

title: Panic Onset Pattern Worksheet
summary: A worksheet mapping the time, place and situation around recent panic attacks to find patterns.
goal: Use it to identify situational patterns that precede a client's panic attacks.
body_md: Log the last several panic attacks with time, place, and what was happening just before, looking for a shared thread, a physical sensation, a place, a type of situation. Some clients find no clear pattern, which is itself useful information about how unpredictable panic can feel. Use whatever pattern emerges to plan targeted practice.

fields.label: When and where did your last panic attack happen?
What was happening right before it started?
Looking at several attacks, is there a shared pattern?
What would you want to practice based on that pattern?

title: Panic Sensation Misinterpretation Log
summary: A log comparing the feared meaning of a body sensation with its actual, harmless explanation.
goal: Use it to challenge catastrophic interpretations of normal panic sensations.
body_md: Panic often runs on a sensation being misread as dangerous, a racing heart read as a heart attack, dizziness read as fainting or worse. List the sensation, the feared interpretation, and a more accurate, harmless explanation grounded in what is known about the body's alarm response. Complete this in session rather than assigning it as homework during an actual panic episode.

fields.label: What body sensation shows up during panic?
What do you fear it means in that moment?
What is a more accurate explanation for that sensation?
How does the accurate explanation change how you respond?

title: Willing to Feel the Wave Practice
summary: A willingness exercise practicing making room for panic sensations rather than fighting them.
goal: Use it to build willingness to let a panic sensation be present without struggling against it.
body_md: The struggle against a panic sensation often intensifies it more than the sensation itself; this exercise practices making room instead. Guide the client to notice the sensation's exact location and shape, then breathe around it rather than trying to push it away. This is a willingness practice for session use, not a stand-alone crisis skill.

fields.label: Where in your body does panic usually show up first?
Without trying to change it, what shape or size does it have?
Practice breathing around it rather than fighting it. What happened?
What is different about making room for it versus fighting it?

title: Supporting Someone Through Panic Conversation
summary: A conversation guide for a partner to learn what actually helps during the other's panic attacks.
goal: Use it to replace a partner's guesswork with what the client has found actually helps.
body_md: Partners often default to over-asking questions or urging someone to calm down, both of which can make panic worse. This conversation has the client name specifically what helps and what does not, so the supporting partner has clear, tested guidance instead of guesswork. Revisit it, since what helps can change over time.

fields.label: What has actually helped you during a past panic attack?
What has made it worse, even if well intended?
Partner: what is one thing you can do next time, based on this?
What should the partner avoid doing?

title: Panic Facts Quick-Fire Trivia Game
summary: A quick trivia game testing accurate facts about what panic attacks are and are not.
goal: Use it to reinforce accurate, calming facts about panic in a playful, low-stakes format.
body_md: Write a set of true-or-false statements about panic, such as whether it can cause fainting or lasts forever, and have players answer quickly before revealing the accurate answer. This reinforces psychoeducation in a lighter format than a straight lecture, which some clients absorb better. Follow any surprising answer with a short explanation.

fields.label: True or false: panic attacks can cause a heart attack.
True or false: panic attacks typically peak and pass within minutes.
True or false: avoiding a place forever makes panic less likely there.
Which answer surprised you most?

title: Parent Self-Care Minimum Worksheet
summary: A worksheet identifying the smallest realistic version of self-care a stretched parent can sustain.
goal: Use it to set a genuinely sustainable floor for a parent's own basic needs.
body_md: Ambitious self-care plans tend to fail for parents with little spare time; this worksheet aims lower on purpose, at the smallest version that could actually happen most days. Ask what has been dropped entirely and which of those matters most to restore first. A five-minute version of something is far better than an abandoned hour-long version.

fields.label: What self-care have you dropped since becoming, or while being, a parent?
Which one matters most to restore?
What is the smallest version of it that could fit into most days?
What would need to be true for that to actually happen?

title: Parent Guilt Thought Challenge
summary: A worksheet examining a guilty parenting thought against the evidence of what actually happened.
goal: Use it to test whether a guilty parenting thought fits the actual facts.
body_md: Parenting guilt often runs on an all-or-nothing standard, one hard moment taken as proof of being a bad parent overall. Walk through the specific evidence for and against that conclusion, including what the parent did well in the same stretch of time. This is not about excusing harmful behavior, only about testing an unfairly harsh verdict.

fields.label: What guilty thought have you had about your parenting recently?
What evidence supports that thought?
What evidence goes against it?
What is a fairer way to think about the situation?

title: Parenting Values in Hard Moments Practice
summary: An exercise connecting a parent's stated values to how they want to respond in a hard moment.
goal: Use it to plan a values-guided response before the next hard parenting moment arrives.
body_md: Ask what kind of parent the client wants to be in the moments that are hardest, not the easy ones, since values show up most clearly under pressure. Compare that to how a recent hard moment actually went, without judgment, then plan one small shift for next time. This works well alongside any parenting skills training already underway.

fields.label: What kind of parent do you want to be in a hard moment?
Describe a recent hard moment. How did it actually go?
What is the gap between the two?
What is one small shift you could try next time?

title: Family Job Chart Craft
summary: A craft where a child helps design a chore chart with age-appropriate family jobs.
goal: Use it to give a child ownership over their contribution to the household.
body_md: Let the child choose from a short list of age-appropriate jobs and decorate the chart themselves, which builds buy-in beyond a chart the parent simply assigns. Keep expectations realistic for the child's age, and pair the chart with parent follow-through and specific praise rather than only consequences. Review and adjust it together every few weeks.

fields.label: Which family jobs do you want to be in charge of?
How will you know when a job is done well?
Decorate your chart.
Parent: how will you notice and praise these jobs getting done?

title: Family Feud Fair Rules Game
summary: A family game where the group votes on fair house rules for common daily flashpoints.
goal: Use it to build buy-in for house rules by involving the whole family in setting them.
body_md: Present a common flashpoint, like screen time or bedtime, and have each family member propose a rule before the group votes on a version everyone can live with. Kids tend to follow rules they helped shape far more than ones handed down. Keep the tone playful, like a game show, to lower defensiveness on all sides.

fields.label: What is a household situation that often causes conflict?
Each person proposes a rule for it.
Vote on a version everyone can accept.
How will the family check in on whether it is working?

title: Postpartum Identity Shift Worksheet
summary: A worksheet exploring what has changed and what remains in a new parent's sense of self.
goal: Use it to name the identity shift of new parenthood without treating it as pure loss.
body_md: New parenthood reshapes identity fast, and clients can feel disoriented without language for what has changed. Ask what has been set aside, what remains, and what is genuinely new and wanted, holding space for grief and gain existing side by side. Avoid rushing to reassurance before the client has had room to name the shift honestly.

fields.label: What part of yourself feels set aside right now?
What part of yourself still feels present?
What is new about who you are that you did not expect?
What would help you feel more like yourself again, even briefly?

title: Postpartum Expectation vs Reality Log
summary: A log comparing what a new parent expected postpartum life to look like against how it actually looks.
goal: Use it to close the gap between an idealized expectation and lived reality without judgment.
body_md: Many new parents carry an unspoken expectation, often shaped by others' curated stories, that sets up a painful comparison to their own harder reality. Write both columns honestly, then ask where the expectation came from and whether it was ever realistic. This is not about lowering hope, only about correcting an unfair standard.

fields.label: What did you expect postpartum life would be like?
What has it actually been like?
Where did that expectation come from?
How would a more realistic expectation change how you judge yourself?

title: Present Moment With Baby Practice
summary: A brief present-moment exercise for connecting with a baby amid exhaustion and racing thoughts.
goal: Use it to practice brief moments of present-moment contact with a baby despite fatigue.
body_md: Exhaustion and intrusive worry can pull a new parent's attention away from the baby in front of them even during quiet moments. Guide a short practice noticing the baby's weight, sound, or smell without needing to feel a particular way about it. This is about brief contact, not manufacturing feelings that are not there yet.

fields.label: Notice the weight or warmth of your baby right now, or imagine a recent moment.
Notice one sound your baby makes.
What thoughts pulled your attention away?
What was it like to come back to the present moment, even briefly?

title: Postpartum Support Request Script
summary: A script for a new parent to ask directly for specific help rather than hoping a partner notices.
goal: Use it to replace vague hoping for help with a direct, specific request.
body_md: New parents often wait to be noticed rather than asking directly, then feel resentful when help does not arrive. Coach a specific, concrete request, what, when, and how, rather than a general complaint about being tired. The supporting partner practices responding to the specific ask rather than a vague sense that something is wrong.

fields.label: What specific task do you need help with this week?
When would that help make the biggest difference?
Practice asking directly, in one or two sentences.
Partner: what is your response to that specific request?

title: Welcoming the Baby Family Craft
summary: A craft for an older sibling to make a welcome item for a new baby, easing the transition.
goal: Use it to give an older sibling a positive, active role in welcoming a new baby.
body_md: An older sibling adjusting to a new baby often needs a concrete way to feel included rather than displaced. Have them make something for the baby, a drawing, a small toy, or a card, and talk through what their new "big sibling" job will be. Parents can use this as an opening to name and validate any mixed feelings the sibling has too.

fields.label: What will you make or draw to welcome the new baby?
What is one job you want to have as a big sibling?
What feels exciting about being a big sibling?
What feels hard or confusing about it?

title: Personal Standards Fairness Audit
summary: A worksheet comparing the standard a client holds themselves to against one they would offer a friend.
goal: Use it to notice a double standard between self-judgment and how a client treats others.
body_md: Clients with low self-esteem often hold a much harsher standard for themselves than for anyone else. List a recent self-critical moment, then ask what standard was actually applied, and whether that same standard would be applied to a friend in the same spot. The gap, once visible, is often the most persuasive part of the exercise.

fields.label: Describe a recent moment you judged yourself harshly.
What standard were you holding yourself to?
Would you hold a friend to that same standard? Why or why not?
What is a fairer standard for yourself?

title: Evidence Against the Inner Critic Worksheet
summary: A worksheet gathering specific counter-evidence against a client's harshest self-belief.
goal: Use it to build a concrete evidence file against an entrenched negative self-belief.
body_md: Name the core negative belief plainly, then spend the bulk of the time gathering specific, concrete counter-evidence rather than generic positive statements. Weak, vague evidence rarely dents a strongly held belief, so push for detail and dates where possible. Keep the finished list somewhere the client can add to it over time.

fields.label: What is the harshest belief you hold about yourself?
List three specific moments that contradict that belief, with detail.
What would someone who knows you well say about that belief?
How strongly do you believe it now, 0 to 100, compared to before?

title: Self as More Than One Story Practice
summary: An exercise widening a client's self-story beyond one dominant negative narrative.
goal: Use it to notice that a client is more than any single story they tell about themselves.
body_md: Clients with low self-esteem often carry one dominant story, like "I am not good enough," that crowds out every other truth about them. Have the client name that story, then list other true stories that also exist alongside it, without needing to erase the first one. The goal is not replacing the story but holding it alongside others.

fields.label: What is the dominant story you tell about yourself?
What is another true story about you that also exists?
And another?
What is it like to hold more than one story at once?

title: Proud Moments Jar Craft
summary: A craft where a child decorates a jar and fills it over time with small proud moments.
goal: Use it to build a visible, growing collection of a child's own proud moments.
body_md: Decorate the jar together in the first session, then send it home with a stack of small paper slips for the child to add to whenever something makes them proud, big or small. A parent can prompt gently at day's end if the child forgets. Bring the jar back in future sessions to read a few slips together.

fields.label: Decorate your jar.
Write or draw one thing you are proud of right now to start it off.
Parent: how will you remind your child to add to the jar?
What do you hope the jar looks like in a month?

title: Strength Charades Game
summary: A charades game where players act out a personal strength for others to guess.
goal: Use it to make naming personal strengths active and fun rather than a quiet list.
body_md: Write a list of strengths, kind, brave, funny, patient, on cards, and have players act one out without words for the group to guess. Afterward, ask each player to name a time they showed that strength themselves. This works well in groups where members may be reluctant to name their own strengths unprompted.

fields.label: Pick a strength card and act it out.
What strength did you guess for others?
Name a time you showed one of these strengths yourself.
Which strength would you like to use more often?

title: Post-Social Review Bias Check
summary: A worksheet comparing a client's harsh post-event self-review against what an observer likely saw.
goal: Use it to correct an overly harsh internal replay of a social interaction.
body_md: After a social event, clients with social anxiety often replay a self-critical highlight reel that does not match how an outside observer likely experienced the same moment. Write both versions side by side, and if possible, ask a trusted person for their honest recollection to compare. The gap between the two versions is usually the point that lands.

fields.label: Describe a recent social moment you have been replaying critically.
What is your harshest version of what happened?
What would a neutral observer likely have noticed instead?
What does comparing the two tell you?

title: Safety Behavior Identification Worksheet
summary: A worksheet identifying the small safety behaviors a client uses to get through social situations.
goal: Use it to surface hidden safety behaviors that quietly maintain social anxiety.
body_md: Safety behaviors are often subtle, rehearsing lines in advance, avoiding eye contact, standing near an exit, and clients rarely notice them as a category until asked directly. List several, then rate how much each one seems to help versus how much it might be preventing the client from learning the feared outcome will not happen. This sets up later work on dropping them one at a time.

fields.label: What small things do you do to get through social situations more easily?
How much does each one seem to help, 0 to 10?
What might each one be preventing you from learning?
Which one would you consider dropping first?

title: Willing to Be Seen Practice
summary: A willingness exercise practicing being visible in a small social moment without hiding.
goal: Use it to build willingness to be seen, awkwardness included, in a small social moment.
body_md: Pick a small, low-stakes moment of being seen, speaking up once in a group, holding eye contact briefly, and have the client practice it while making room for the discomfort rather than trying to eliminate it first. The point is not comfort but willingness. Debrief on what it was like to act despite the discomfort, not whether the discomfort went away.

fields.label: What small moment of being seen will you practice?
What discomfort do you expect to show up?
Practice it while making room for that discomfort. What happened?
What did you learn about acting despite discomfort?

title: Social Effort Pacing Card
summary: A card for pacing social exposure practice so it builds skill without overwhelming the client.
goal: Use it to balance stretching a client's social comfort zone against burning out on effort.
body_md: Too much social exposure practice too fast can lead a client to quit altogether; this card helps calibrate a sustainable pace. Rate the planned social effort for the week, then check in on energy and willingness afterward before planning the next one. Some weeks call for pulling back, not just pushing forward.

fields.label: What social effort are you planning this week?
How much energy do you expect it to take, 0 to 10?
After trying it, how did your energy and willingness hold up?
Should next week be a stretch, a repeat, or a step back?

title: Two-Minute Conversation Challenge Game
summary: A timed practice game for holding a light two-minute conversation on a randomly drawn topic.
goal: Use it to build low-stakes practice holding a short conversation to completion.
body_md: Draw a light topic card, like a favorite show or a recent weekend, and set a timer for two minutes of conversation, in-session with the clinician or between group members. The short time limit lowers the stakes, since a conversation only has to last two minutes rather than feel indefinite. Debrief on what felt easier or harder than expected.

fields.label: Draw a topic card and set a two-minute timer.
How did the conversation feel while it was happening?
What was easier than you expected?
What would you want to practice next?

title: Grief Bursts Mapping Worksheet
summary: A worksheet mapping when and where unexpected waves of grief tend to show up.
goal: Use it to help a client anticipate and plan for sudden grief bursts rather than being blindsided.
body_md: Grief often arrives in short, intense bursts triggered by ordinary things, a song, a smell, a date, rather than as a steady state. Map recent bursts by trigger and setting to look for a pattern, and identify one or two upcoming situations likely to bring one on. Planning does not prevent the burst, but it makes it feel less like an ambush.

fields.label: Describe a recent moment grief hit unexpectedly.
What triggered it?
Is there a pattern across recent bursts?
What upcoming situation might bring one on, and how could you prepare?

title: If-Only Thought Fairness Check
summary: A worksheet testing a guilt-driven "if only" thought against what the client actually knew at the time.
goal: Use it to test a hindsight-driven guilty thought against realistic knowledge at the time.
body_md: If-only thoughts judge past decisions using information only available in hindsight, which is not a fair standard. Write the thought, then ask what the client actually knew and could have reasonably predicted at that exact moment, not what is obvious now. This does not erase grief, but it can loosen guilt that is not warranted by the facts.

fields.label: What "if only" thought keeps coming up?
What did you actually know at that time, before it happened?
Could you have reasonably predicted the outcome with that information?
What is a fairer way to look at the decision you made?

title: Carrying Grief and Living Practice
summary: An exercise exploring how to carry grief alongside continuing to live and engage with values.
goal: Use it to explore carrying grief and moving toward values as compatible, not opposed.
body_md: Some clients feel that moving forward means betraying the person or life they lost, which can keep them stuck between grieving and living. Frame carrying grief and continuing to act on values as two things that can coexist rather than compete. Ask what the person they lost might want for them, if that framing feels right to the client.

fields.label: What does moving forward feel like it would mean or betray?
What value do you want to keep living out, even while grieving?
What would carrying both grief and this value look like, together?
What is one small step in that direction?

title: Grieving Differently as a Couple Conversation
summary: A conversation guide for partners grieving the same loss in visibly different ways.
goal: Use it to help partners understand and accept each other's different grieving style.
body_md: Partners often grieve the same loss differently, one more outwardly emotional, one more private or task-focused, and can misread each other's style as not caring. Have each partner describe their own style and what they need, then reflect back what they heard before responding. Naming the difference as different, not wrong, tends to ease tension.

fields.label: How does grief tend to show up for you?
What do you need from your partner right now?
Partner: what did you hear, and how did that surprise you, if at all?
What would it look like to respect each other's different style?

title: Special Memory Keepsake Box Craft
summary: A craft where a child decorates a small box to hold objects and drawings connected to someone they lost.
goal: Use it to give a child a concrete, ongoing way to hold onto memories of someone they lost.
body_md: Let the child decorate the box however they like, then help them choose or draw a few small items connected to the person they lost, a photo, a drawing, a small object. This gives a concrete place for memories rather than asking a child to hold grief only in words. A parent can help add to the box over time as the child wants.

fields.label: Decorate your memory box.
What will you put inside it to start?
What is one memory you want to remember about this person?
Where will you keep your box at home?

title: Relationship Deal-Breakers and Preferences Sheet
summary: A worksheet sorting relationship concerns into genuine deal-breakers versus flexible preferences.
goal: Use it to clarify which relationship concerns are firm limits versus areas open to compromise.
body_md: Clients sometimes treat every friction point in a relationship as equally serious, which makes every disagreement feel high-stakes. Sort a list of current concerns into genuine deal-breakers and preferences that could flex with negotiation. This distinction alone often lowers the temperature of ongoing conflict.

fields.label: List your current concerns in the relationship.
Which of these are true deal-breakers for you?
Which are preferences you could negotiate on?
What does that sorting change about how you want to approach them?

title: Relationship Story Rewrite Worksheet
summary: A worksheet rewriting a fixed negative story about a partner with more recent, balanced evidence.
goal: Use it to update an outdated or overly fixed negative narrative about a partner.
body_md: Long relationships sometimes carry a frozen story about a partner, formed years ago, that does not update even as the partner changes. Write the old story, then gather recent evidence for and against it. The goal is not blind positivity but an accurate, current picture rather than an outdated one.

fields.label: What is the fixed story you carry about your partner?
When did that story form?
What recent evidence supports or contradicts it?
What would an updated, current story sound like?

title: Interpersonal Priorities Triage Card
summary: A card for weighing objective, relationship and self-respect priorities before a hard conversation.
goal: Use it to plan a hard conversation by weighing what matters most before it happens.
body_md: Before a difficult conversation, have the client weigh three things: getting the objective outcome, protecting the relationship, and keeping their own self-respect, since a plan usually has to trade off between them. Naming the priority in advance prevents the conversation from drifting into whichever goal feels loudest in the moment. Revisit the card afterward to see how the actual conversation matched the plan.

fields.label: What is the objective outcome you want from this conversation?
How important is protecting the relationship in this moment?
How important is your own self-respect here?
Given all three, what is your plan going in?

title: Unspoken Expectations Reveal
summary: An exercise where partners write and compare unspoken expectations they have been carrying.
goal: Use it to surface expectations partners assume are shared but have never actually stated.
body_md: Many relationship frictions trace back to an expectation one partner assumed was obvious or shared, but never actually said out loud. Have each partner write a few unspoken expectations privately before comparing, since some overlap and some genuinely surprise the other partner. Turn any real mismatches into explicit agreements rather than leaving them assumed again.

fields.label: Write two or three expectations you have been assuming, without saying them.
Partner: write your own, separately.
Compare lists. What overlapped? What surprised you?
Which mismatch is worth turning into an explicit agreement?

title: Relationship Trivia: How Well Do You Know Me Now
summary: A trivia game where partners guess each other's current preferences, which often drift over time.
goal: Use it to playfully update partners' knowledge of each other, since people change over time.
body_md: Long-term partners often rely on outdated knowledge of each other; this game has each partner guess the other's current favorite, worry, or hope, then check the answer. Wrong guesses are the useful part, since they reveal where a couple's knowledge of each other has drifted. Keep it light and curious rather than turning wrong answers into criticism.

fields.label: Partner A guesses Partner B's current biggest stressor, then B reveals the real answer.
Partner B guesses Partner A's current favorite way to relax, then A reveals the real answer.
What surprised you about the answers?
What is one way to keep learning about each other going forward?

title: Body Signals Safety Check Worksheet
summary: A worksheet for noticing current body signals of safety versus alarm, in the present moment.
goal: Use it to build a client's awareness of present-moment body safety signals.
body_md: Keep this entirely present-focused: what the body is signaling right now, not a review of past events. This is a stabilizing awareness tool, useful before or alongside grounding work, never an invitation to recount what happened. Complete this in session rather than sending it home as unsupervised work.

fields.label: What does your body feel like right now, in this moment?
What tells you that you are safe right now?
Is there any tension or alarm present? Where?
What would help your body settle further right now?

title: Self-Blame Responsibility Sorting Worksheet
summary: A worksheet sorting responsibility for what happened away from the client and onto the person responsible.
goal: Use it to correct misplaced self-blame by sorting out where responsibility actually lies.
body_md: Self-blame is extremely common after sexual abuse and rarely reflects the actual facts of responsibility. Without asking the client to describe what happened, work with the belief itself: what they believe they are responsible for, and whether that belief holds up against basic facts about consent and power. Go slowly, and stop if the client becomes flooded.

fields.label: What do you believe you are responsible for?
What facts about consent or power apply here?
Who holds responsibility for what happened, based on those facts?
What is it like to consider that belief may not be accurate?

title: Present-Moment Anchoring Skills Card
summary: A reference card of quick anchoring skills to use when a client feels pulled out of the present.
goal: Use it to give a client fast, reliable ways to return to the present moment.
body_md: List several concrete anchoring skills, cold water, naming objects in the room, pressing feet into the floor, and have the client rate which ones work fastest for them personally. Practice each one in session so it is familiar before it is needed in a harder moment. This card is a stabilizing tool, meant for daily and in-the-moment use, not a substitute for a full safety plan.

fields.label: Which anchoring skill worked fastest for you when we practiced it?
Where will you keep this card so it is easy to find?
What situations might call for using it?
What is your backup skill if the first one does not work?

title: Partner Pacing and Consent Check-In
summary: A check-in structure for a couple to communicate pace and consent around physical intimacy.
goal: Use it to build a clear, ongoing way for both partners to communicate about pace and consent.
body_md: Build a simple, explicit way to check in before and during physical intimacy, a word or signal either partner can use without needing to explain. Keep the conversation about comfort, pace and consent, never a request to discuss what happened. The non-affected partner often needs coaching that patience here is a form of care, not a problem to solve.

fields.label: What check-in signal or word will you use together?
What does "yes, keep going" look like for you?
What does "let's pause" look like for you?
Partner: how will you respond when the pause signal comes up?

title: Body Belongs to Me Safety Rules Craft
summary: A craft where a child decorates a poster of simple body safety rules with trusted grown-ups.
goal: Use it to reinforce clear, simple body safety rules a child can remember and use.
body_md: Keep the language simple and rule-based, my body belongs to me, I can say no, I can tell a safe grown-up, rather than any detailed or frightening explanation. If a child discloses anything during this activity, pause and follow your state's mandatory reporting duties before continuing. Send the finished poster home and review the safe-adults list with the parent.

fields.label: Decorate your body safety rules poster.
Write or draw the safe grown-ups you could tell if something felt wrong.
Practice saying "no" out loud.
What is one safe grown-up you could go to today?

title: Coping Skills Cost and Access Matrix
summary: A worksheet sorting a client's coping skills by how much effort they take and how accessible they are.
goal: Use it to build a realistic coping plan sorted by effort and accessibility, not just preference.
body_md: A coping skill that is technically effective but requires too much setup often goes unused in a real hard moment. Sort skills into a simple grid by effort required and how accessible they are anywhere, anytime versus only at home. Make sure at least a few low-effort, high-access options are always on hand.

fields.label: List coping skills that work for you, regardless of effort.
Which ones are low effort and available almost anywhere?
Which ones take more setup or only work at home?
What is your go-to option for a hard moment in public?

title: Unhelpful Coping Pattern Swap Worksheet
summary: A worksheet identifying an unhelpful coping habit and planning a healthier swap for the same function.
goal: Use it to replace an unhelpful coping habit with one that serves the same function.
body_md: Rather than simply telling a client to stop an unhelpful habit, identify what function it serves, distraction, comfort, control, and find a swap that serves the same function without the same cost. A direct swap tends to stick better than a replacement chosen at random. Expect some trial and error before finding a good match.

fields.label: What is a coping habit you would like to change?
What function does it serve, like comfort or distraction?
What is another way to meet that same function?
How did trying the swap go?

title: Coping With Willingness, Not Elimination Practice
summary: An exercise reframing coping skills as tools for carrying discomfort, not eliminating it.
goal: Use it to shift the goal of coping from eliminating discomfort to carrying it workably.
body_md: Clients sometimes judge a coping skill as failing whenever discomfort remains afterward, when many skills are meant to help a person function alongside discomfort, not erase it. Reframe the goal explicitly: did this skill help you keep moving with the discomfort present, rather than did it make the discomfort disappear. This often reduces frustration with skills that were actually working.

fields.label: What coping skill have you judged as "not working"?
Did it help you keep functioning, even with discomfort still present?
What would "success" look like if the goal is carrying discomfort, not erasing it?
Does that change how you feel about the skill?

title: Personal Crisis Skill Hierarchy Card
summary: A card ranking a client's coping skills from mild distress up through crisis-level distress.
goal: Use it to give a client a ranked plan of skills matched to distress intensity, including crisis level.
body_md: Build the hierarchy together from mild through severe distress, and for the top of the scale, include a plan for reaching out, a trusted person, a crisis line, or 988, which can be called or texted. Complete this in session, walking through what the client would actually do at each level, rather than assigning it as homework. Keep the finished card somewhere easy to find.

fields.label: What skill works for mild distress, 1 to 3 out of 10?
What skill works for moderate distress, 4 to 6?
What skill works for high distress, 7 to 8?
At a 9 or 10, or if you are unsafe, who will you call or text, including 988 if needed?

title: Coping Skills Speed Sort Game
summary: A timed sorting game racing to sort coping skill cards into correct categories before time runs out.
goal: Use it to build quick, confident recall of which coping skills fit which category.
body_md: Shuffle a deck of coping skill cards and set a timer for sorting them into categories like calming, distracting, and connecting with others. Speed adds a playful pressure that helps skills become more automatic to recall. Play multiple rounds, timing improvement rather than perfection, and debrief on any cards that were genuinely tricky to sort.

fields.label: Sort your coping skill cards into categories before time runs out.
How long did it take you?
Which card was hardest to sort? Why?
Which category has the fewest cards? What could you add?

title: Phobia Avoidance Ripple Effect Worksheet
summary: A worksheet mapping how avoiding a feared object or situation has quietly shrunk a client's life.
goal: Use it to make the widening cost of avoidance visible beyond the feared situation itself.
body_md: A phobia's cost often extends well past the feared object itself, into missed events, altered routes, or avoided plans that ripple outward. List the direct avoidance first, then trace what it has affected further out. Seeing the full ripple, not just the original fear, often builds stronger motivation for exposure work than the fear alone.

fields.label: What do you avoid directly because of this fear?
What has that avoidance affected beyond the fear itself?
And beyond that?
What would you want back if the ripple effect were smaller?

title: Fear Probability Estimate Worksheet
summary: A worksheet comparing a client's estimated probability of the feared outcome with a realistic estimate.
goal: Use it to challenge an inflated probability estimate of the feared outcome actually occurring.
body_md: Phobias often inflate the actual likelihood of harm far beyond what is realistic. Have the client estimate the probability of the feared outcome, then walk through available information to build a more realistic estimate, and revisit both numbers after any approach step is attempted. The gap between feared and actual probability tends to shrink with repeated practice.

fields.label: What is the feared outcome?
What probability do you give it happening, 0 to 100?
What does the available information suggest is more realistic?
After trying an approach step, how did the numbers compare?

title: Willing to Feel Afraid and Approach Practice
summary: A willingness exercise separating the presence of fear from the decision to approach anyway.
goal: Use it to practice approaching a feared situation while fear is still present, not after it is gone.
body_md: Clients often wait for fear to go away before approaching a feared situation, which can delay action indefinitely. Practice the distinction directly: fear can be present at the same time as a chosen approach step, rather than one needing to precede the other. Use a low-stakes approach step to practice this distinction concretely.

fields.label: What approach step are you willing to try, fear and all?
How much fear do you expect to feel, 0 to 10?
Try the step while making room for that fear. What happened?
What did you learn about acting alongside fear rather than after it?

title: Brave Steps Sticker Map Craft
summary: A craft where a child builds and decorates a map of approach steps toward a feared object.
goal: Use it to give a child a visual, rewarding path through graded approach steps.
body_md: Build the map together as a path with a handful of steps, from easiest to the goal step, and let the child decorate it and choose stickers to earn along the way. A parent should be part of planning how and when steps get practiced at home, with praise for effort, not just success. Keep the pace led by the child's readiness, not a fixed schedule.

fields.label: Draw your path with a few steps from easy to brave.
Decorate your map.
Which step will you try first?
Parent: how will you support and celebrate each step?

title: Feared Object Fact Hunt Game
summary: A game where players search for and share accurate facts about a feared object or animal.
goal: Use it to build accurate knowledge about a feared object in a playful, curious format.
body_md: Have players find or share interesting, accurate facts about the feared object or animal, taking turns presenting one fact at a time. Curiosity and fact-finding can loosen a fear's grip in a way that stays lighter than direct exposure alone. This works especially well for children fearful of animals or natural phenomena.

fields.label: Share one fact you found about the feared object or animal.
What surprised you about that fact?
Did learning it change how scary the object feels, even a little?
What is one more fact you would like to learn?

title: Appearance-Free Day Reflection Worksheet
summary: A worksheet reflecting on a day spent minimizing appearance-checking behaviors.
goal: Use it to build awareness of how much attention appearance normally takes up.
body_md: Ask the client to notice, for one day, how often attention pulls toward appearance, mirrors, reflections, comparing to others, without any requirement to change the behavior yet. This is an awareness exercise, not a challenge to pass or fail, and some clients find the sheer frequency surprising once counted. Use the reflection to choose one behavior to work on next.

fields.label: Roughly how many times did your attention pull toward appearance today?
What situations triggered it most?
What did you notice about how that attention affected your mood?
What is one behavior you would like to work on reducing?

title: Appearance Rule Origin Worksheet
summary: A worksheet tracing where a rigid appearance-related rule or standard originally came from.
goal: Use it to examine a rigid appearance rule by tracing its origin and current cost.
body_md: Rigid appearance rules, like needing to look a certain way before leaving the house, usually have a traceable origin, a comment, a comparison, a message absorbed early. Naming the origin often loosens the rule's grip, since it reveals the rule as learned rather than an objective truth. Keep the conversation on function and rules, never on specific numbers or measurements.

fields.label: What is a rigid rule you hold about your appearance?
Where do you think that rule first came from?
What does following that rule cost you day to day?
What would a more flexible version of that rule look like?

title: Body as Instrument Practice
summary: An exercise shifting focus from how the body looks to what the body allows a client to do.
goal: Use it to shift attention from appearance toward the body's function in a client's life.
body_md: Ask the client to list what their body allows them to do, hug someone, walk outside, laugh, rather than how it looks. This keeps the exercise strictly on function and capability, never on weight, size, or appearance. Some clients find this shift difficult at first; normalize that it takes repeated practice to redirect attention this way.

fields.label: What does your body allow you to do that matters to you?
What has your body carried you through?
How does focusing on function feel different from focusing on appearance?
What is one way to notice your body's function this week?

title: Supporting Body Image Without Commenting Conversation
summary: A conversation guide helping a partner support body image struggles without commenting on appearance.
goal: Use it to agree on supportive language that leaves appearance and food entirely out of it.
body_md: Well-meaning comments about appearance, even compliments, can reinforce a preoccupation with how the body looks. Coach the supporting partner toward comments about presence, effort or connection instead, and explicitly agree to keep appearance and food out of the conversation altogether. Revisit the agreement if old habits creep back in.

fields.label: What kinds of comments about your appearance feel unhelpful, even if well meant?
What kind of support actually feels helpful?
Partner: what will you say instead, going forward?
What will you both do if an old habit slips back in?

title: All the Things My Body Can Do Craft
summary: A craft where a child draws and lists all the things their body can do, like run, hug and draw.
goal: Use it to build a child's sense of their body as capable, not something to judge by looks.
body_md: Have the child trace or draw an outline of themselves and fill it with drawings of activities their body lets them do, playing, hugging, jumping, drawing itself. Keep the activity strictly about capability and fun, with no reference to size, weight or how bodies look. Parents can extend this at home by noticing and naming what the child's body does well.

fields.label: Draw an outline of yourself.
Fill it with pictures of things your body lets you do.
Which of these is your favorite thing your body can do?
What is something new you would like your body to help you try?
